Meeting header:
Date: 2028-01-11
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording id: ff-20280111-kyb-03-recording
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Lina Torres (Kyberon CTO), Jae Park (Kyberon ML Eng), Marco Velez (Kyberon Infra)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):

- Redwood shows lower p95 but some throughput headroom/lower sustained QPS under default batching config
- Network egress and VPC peering contributed to ~30-50ms variance in a couple runs

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: all right, good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, with Ethan on the line as well, how's everyone doing?
[00:12] Lina: hey Maya, good thanks, busy week but excited to see the numbers.
[00:17] Jae: hi all
[00:20] Ethan: hey, morning from my side, we'll jump into the bench outputs, quick agenda — readout, triage where things diverge vs incumbent, and then next steps.
[01:05] Maya: quick housekeeping, recording on — if you have any sensitive snippets flag them and we'll redact in the share.
[01:22] Marco: noted, thanks.
[02:00] Ethan: OK, starting with the p50/p95 table — most representative workload was 1k requests, dialog-like prompts median length ~120 tokens. Redwood runs (quantized) p50 ~82ms, p95 ~290ms under default continuous-batching at 20ms latency target. IncumbentAI baseline p50 ~95ms, p95 ~420ms in their hosted endpoint.
[02:45] Jae: curious, are those numbers from your shared CSV or from their public endpoint?
[02:52] Ethan: those are our lab runs against the baseline test harness — we ran both back-to-back with identical request traces. We recorded 3 windows across different times.
[03:20] Lina: I saw a slide earlier that showed throughput QPS lower for Redwood at sustained load?
[03:27] Ethan: yes, good call — sustained throughput at concurrency 120 was ~340 qps for Redwood in the default config versus ~420 qps for incumbent. The throughput delta appears tied to default batching window and memory pressure on the GPU with our quantization path.
[04:00] Marco: did you pin the kernels / run with cudnn or whatever? We saw some noisy numbers when drivers mismatched.
[04:10] Ethan: right, for the runs we used the standard runtime kernel selection; there was one run where kernel fallback triggered due to a sequence-length spike and that added ~60-80ms tail in that window. We noted that in the CSV.
[05:05] Jae: you mentioned quantization path — is Redwood using 4-bit int or 8-bit mixed?
[05:12] Ethan: for this POC we used the 4-bit q4_0 path for lower memory but that can trade throughput. We also ran a q8/float16 variant which improved throughput to ~390 qps but p95 rose slightly in some tails. It's a tuning tradeoff.
[05:40] Lina: any thoughts on whether dedicated slots would smooth throughput?
[05:46] Ethan: definitely — dedicated GPU pools reduce job prep overhead, avoid kernel churn across tenants, and guarantee slot sizing. For folks with steady traffic we typically recommend 2-4 dedicated slots in early pilot.
[06:30] Maya: can you walk through an example session where Redwood wins on latency but loses on throughput? I want the team to understand operational impact.
[06:38] Ethan: sure — so in our tail-run at 12:32 UTC, Redwood p95 was 270ms vs incumbent 410ms. That run used prefix caching effectively for repeated prompts which reduced token generation overhead. But under a synthetic sustained burst test where the traffic had high diversity (few repeats), our default batching window added latency to coalesce tokens and GPU memory bounded throughput, so QPS lagged.
[07:25] Marco: interesting — sounds like caching benefits are workload-dependent. Our traffic is pretty chatty, but with lots of small unique requests.
[07:33] Jae: that's our main worry — most of our calls are short and unique, like semantic search-ish.
[07:40] Ethan: okay so recommendations: for unique short requests we adjust batching target to lower coalescing delay (e.g., set 5ms target) and switch to q8 or f16 for throughput-critical endpoints. Also enable prefix-KV caching where applicable.
[08:10] Lina: any change to cost estimates with those moves?
[08:14] Ethan: yes, moving to q8/f16 increases memory/op cost but improves QPS; cost per token may go up a bit but cost per request can drop due to fewer retries and lower overall latency SLA penalties. We'll surface numbers in the CSV.
[09:00] Maya: let's talk about the network variance you called out. Marco, you said there were VPC peering rules that might have influenced a run?
[09:10] Marco: yeah we had one window where peering went over a transit node because of a misconfigured route, added ~35ms median to that window. I fixed the rule after the run.
[09:28] Ethan: we marked that window in the logs; removing it raises our p50/p95 slightly better. Still, even excluding that, Redwood p95 remained materially lower in most steady windows.
[10:05] Jae: on the CSV I noticed some mislabeled columns — "KVcash" instead of KV cache — small transcription note but the data's fine.
[10:12] Ethan: haha yeah, our auto-exporter sometimes mangles field names. We'll send a cleaned CSV.
[11:00] Lina: can you summarize the key delta numbers we should care about?
[11:05] Ethan: short: p50 delta ~13ms favoring Redwood; p95 delta ~130ms favoring Redwood; sustained throughput gap ~-80 to -40 qps depending on quant path; unit cost per 1k requests comparable after quantization and batching tuning.
[12:10] Marco: does Redwood's scheduler support a mixed routing policy — e.g., send 20% to incumbent as failover?
[12:18] Maya: yes, we can configure smart routing — by latency, cost, region, or a canary percent. We recommend a gradually increasing canary and automated fallback on errors.
[12:45] Jae: any constraints for SSO/SAML or SOC2 docs? Our security team will need SOC2 Type II and audit logs.
[12:54] Maya: we have SOC2 Type II, ISO in progress; we also provide audit logs, SSO SAML integrations, RBAC, and optional customer-managed KMS for Private deployments. We'll share the security pack.
[13:30] Lina: great — for the pilot we need to validate encryption at rest and in transit.
[13:35] Ethan: confirmed — our default hosted path is TLS in transit, and we can enable customer KMS for keys; for Private we can run on your VPC.
[14:20] Marco: back to perf: did you try a run with pre-warmed KV caches across sessions?
[14:28] Ethan: yes, pre-warm cache tests improved p50 by ~10-20ms on repeat-heavy workloads. The challenge is for stateless short-unique workloads there isn't much cache hit rate.
[15:10] Jae: curious if we can run a hybrid: route short-unique to incumbent and reuse Redwood where prompts show repetition?
[15:18] Maya: that's exactly where smart routing helps — you can route by signature of request or by observed hit-rate. We'll help instrument that.
[16:05] Ethan: quick note on quantization: our q4 path reduces memory but increases kernel overhead in some model ops; in some spots that overhead lowers throughput. So q8/f16 is a middle ground.
[16:40] Marco: any plan to test different instance types for the dedicated slots? e.g., larger GPU with more memory to keep it all in faster memory?
[16:47] Ethan: we can spin a 80GB variant for trials; that tends to reduce kernel swapping and improves sustained QPS. We'll propose two slot types in the pricing doc.
[17:30] Lina: will you be able to share the run-level logs so our infra folks can do correlation?
[17:36] Ethan: yes, we'll share full run logs and also the per-request traces (redacted) and the Jupyter that reproduces the charts.
[18:10] Jae: timeline-wise, if we get the CSV and do the network test next week, when can we expect a tuned pilot?
[18:18] Maya: optimistic — 2 weeks after network validation we can stand up dedicated slots and run a new head-to-head. So tentative mid-late Jan.
[19:00] Marco: any blockers from Redwood side on data residency? Some regulatory constraints in EU.
[19:08] Maya: we can pin region and also offer Private deployment for EU data residency. We'll include that option in SOW.
[20:00] Lina: a few clarifying Qs from our side: 1) can Redwood show p99 numbers? 2) costs if we run continuous 24/7 vs burst only?
[20:12] Ethan: yes we'll extract p99 and provide cost delta for 24/7 reserved vs burst-on-demand. We'll include a scenario analysis.
[21:00] Maya: ok time to recap — Ethan will share raw CSV and notebook by Friday (2028-01-13), Marco sends network config and firewall rules by Saturday (2028-01-14), Redwood to draft pricing/slot SOW by 2028-01-20; Kyberon to confirm representative 1k trace by 2028-01-14.
[21:40] Jae: sounds good. One more ask — can you also include the exact invocation payloads for the failing runs?
[21:48] Ethan: yes, we can include anonymized payloads.
[22:30] Lina: great thanks everyone, appreciate the deep dive.
[22:40] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links.
[45:30] Meeting end
